about.title: Ontario Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Ontario sits where three freeways meet, and much of the local workday happens in motion: on warehouse floors, in loading yards, and behind the wheel along I-10, SR-60, and I-15. When a shift ends with an injury instead of a paycheck, the questions come fast. Who pays for the emergency visit? Will hours get cut for reporting it? Is workers' compensation the only option? Under California law, workers' comp is usually your exclusive remedy against your employer, regardless of who was at fault. It is not always the whole story, though. If a subcontractor, a property owner, a defective piece of equipment, or another driver on Euclid Avenue caused your injury, a separate third-party claim may exist alongside the comp case. That claim carries its own two-year deadline. LawProactive is a free service, not a law firm. We connect Ontario workers with an independent personal injury attorney who can sort out which paths apply. Attorneys in our network work on contingency, so there is no fee unless there is a recovery.

items.question: I was hit by another driver on the I-10 while making deliveries for my Ontario employer. Is that only a workers' comp case?
items.answer: Not necessarily. Because you were working, workers' comp likely covers your medical care and part of your lost wages. Since another driver may have been negligent, a separate third-party injury claim against that driver could also exist. That second claim must be filed within two years, so it helps to have an attorney review it soon.

items.question: How quickly do I need to report a workplace injury in California?
items.answer: You should notify your employer within 30 days of the injury, ideally in writing. Reporting late can complicate your workers' comp benefits. If the injury developed gradually, tell your employer as soon as you connect it to your work.

items.question: Can my employer fire me or cut my hours for filing a claim?
items.answer: No. California law prohibits retaliation against workers who report an injury or file for workers' compensation. If you notice a sudden change in hours, duties, or treatment after reporting, mention it to the attorney you are connected with, because it may be part of your case.
